A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CODECRASH. Their complete main texts, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching content moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 17 LLMs and three reasoning models, perturbation sensitivity experiments, prompting controls and failure case studies.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds variability statistics, more detailed result breakdowns and another failure case study.

M1.justification: The AST processing and validation pipeline and all seven perturbation strategies remain unchanged. V1 Appendix B matches v2 Appendix A; the new contextual-level and reasoning-level terminology classifies existing perturbations.

E1.justification: Both use 800 CRUXEval Python problems for input/output prediction and 479 LiveCodeBench problems from 85 solutions for output prediction. V2's additional breakdowns and case study use this retained coverage; other languages are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: The same 17 LLMs, three reasoning models, o3-mini reasoning-effort configurations and vanilla comparisons are evaluated. The added Claude case examines an already evaluated model without introducing a new comparator.

E3.justification: Dataset sizes, prompting examples, sampling settings, token limits and evaluation metrics are retained. V2 explicitly explains the existing absolute and relative degradation metrics; its additional reporting does not establish a changed experimental protocol.

E4.justification: V2 adds an analysis of stability across sampled answers in Appendix B and a paired vanilla/MHC Claude-3.5-Sonnet case in Appendix E.4, showing an intermediate answer of 4 overridden by 3. Existing density tests, comment-ignoring controls, weighting comparisons and five earlier cases are retained.

E5.justification: V1 states candidate counts without reporting variability estimates. V2 adds standard deviations for 357 direct-inference scores in Tables 8–9 and reports 95.78% agreement of correctness labels across candidates. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting; the stated three direct-inference candidates and one CoT candidate remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Results in all eleven original tables are unchanged. V2 adds dataset-specific CoT results, sampling statistics, a 4/479 QwQ collapse frequency and the Claude override example. Section 4.2.2 also incorrectly reverses the GBC dataset trend despite retaining drops of 7.99 pp on CRUX and 3.89 pp on LCB.

T1.justification: No substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions or proofs change. V2 spells out standard formulas for degradation metrics already used in v1, while retaining the weighted robustness definition.

C1.justification: The central claims about structural fragility, natural-language dependence, CoT benefits and reasoning collapse persist. V2 adds an explicit contribution claim that the framework is easily applicable to other benchmarks and programming languages; its abstract's numerical findings largely summarize existing evidence.

C2.justification: New Appendix F specifies limitations involving Python algorithmic tasks, unevaluated models, PASS@1's omissions and the absence of definitive mitigation strategies. Appendix E.4 adds an interpretation of hints overriding correct intermediate reasoning. Earlier shortcut and self-reflection explanations remain.

D1.justification: V2 changes the stated project location and explicitly includes perturbed datasets among publicly available resources. Appendix F newly states that all prompts and complete responses were recorded. Perturbation templates, evaluation prompts and inference hyperparameters otherwise match.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to natural-language stress testing, code-poisoning research and comment inconsistency through Naik, Wan, Sun and Rong et al., alongside model and tool citations. The main related-work discussion and benchmark positioning remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and results discussion are extensively rewritten. Output analysis is reorganized around levels of natural-language dependence and disorganized code; experimental settings move from Section 3.4 to 4.1. Appendices are reordered and gain a contents page, expanded explanations and navigation.

P2.justification: V2 adds variability tables, dataset-specific CoT tables, absolute-score displays and Claude code/trace panels. The pipeline diagram moves from main-text Figure 1 to appendix Figure 3 and is reformatted. Plot labels, diagram formatting, captions and table placement also change substantially.

improvement.justification: V2 improves transparency through variability estimates, dataset-specific CoT results, a paired failure trace and explicit limitations while preserving the original benchmark evidence. These benefits are tempered by new reporting errors: Section 4.2.2 reverses the GBC dataset comparison, and Appendix B states 57 measurements have sigma above 0.5 although Tables 8–9 contain 68. The additions provide a limited overall gain despite these inaccuracies.
